question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-(x-2){y}^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-2>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=1,\,q(x)=-(x-2),\,n=3.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{-2}=-(x-2).\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-(x-2)
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z=2\cdot (x-2)
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-2,\,Q(x)=2\cdot (x-2)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z) & ={e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}\cdot (2\cdot (x-2)) \\ {e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z{e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)} & =2\cdot (x-2){e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}) & =2\cdot (x-2){e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\cdot (x-2){e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2\cdot (x-2)}(2\cdot (x-2)+1)+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C{e}^{2\cdot (x-2)}-2\cdot (x-2)-1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-2}=\frac{C{e}^{2\cdot (x-2)}-2\cdot (x-2)-1}{2}\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{C{e}^{2\cdot (x-2)}-2\cdot (x-2)-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above.

generation.domains: translated coordinate positive; nonzero real branches; exclude singularities

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{(x-1)}^{2}y={(x-1)}^{2}{y}^{-4}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-1>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-3{(x-1)}^{2},\,q(x)={(x-1)}^{2},\,n=-4.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by ${y}^{4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{4}\frac{dy}{dx}-3{(x-1)}^{2}{y}^{5}={(x-1)}^{2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{5}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=5{y}^{4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3{(x-1)}^{2}z={(x-1)}^{2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-15{(x-1)}^{2}z=5{(x-1)}^{2}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-15{(x-1)}^{2},\,Q(x)=5{(x-1)}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-15{(x-1)}^{2})\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-15{(x-1)}^{2}z) & ={e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}\cdot (5{(x-1)}^{2}) \\ {e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-15{(x-1)}^{2}z{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}} & =5{(x-1)}^{2}{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}) & =5{(x-1)}^{2}{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}})\,\text{d}x & =\int 5{(x-1)}^{2}{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}} & =-\frac{{e}^{-5{(x-1)}^{3}}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C{e}^{5{(x-1)}^{3}}-1}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{5}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{5}=\frac{C{e}^{5{(x-1)}^{3}}-1}{3}\,⇒\,y=\sqrt[5]{\frac{C{e}^{5{(x-1)}^{3}}-1}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above.

generation.domains: translated coordinate positive; nonzero real branches; exclude singularities

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+(x+6)y=(x+6){y}^{2}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x+6>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=(x+6),\,q(x)=(x+6),\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}+(x+6){y}^{-1}=(x+6).\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+(x+6)z=(x+6)
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-(x+6)z=-(x+6)
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-(x+6),\,Q(x)=-(x+6)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-(x+6))\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-(x+6)z) & ={e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}\cdot (-(x+6)) \\ {e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-(x+6)z{e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2} & =-(x+6){e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}) & =-(x+6){e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2})\,\text{d}x & =-\int (x+6){e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2} & ={e}^{-{(x+6)}^{2}/2}+C \\ z & =1+C{e}^{{(x+6)}^{2}/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=1+C{e}^{{(x+6)}^{2}/2}\,⇒\,y=\frac{1}{1+C{e}^{{(x+6)}^{2}/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above.

generation.domains: translated coordinate positive; nonzero real branches; exclude singularities

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{(x+3)}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x+3>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{(x+3)},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{(x+3)}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{(x+3)}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{(x+3)}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{(x+3)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{(x+3)}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x+3)}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{(x+3)}\cdot (-{e}^{(x+3)}) \\ {e}^{(x+3)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{(x+3)} & =-{e}^{2\cdot (x+3)} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{(x+3)}) & =-{e}^{2\cdot (x+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{(x+3)})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2\cdot (x+3)}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{(x+3)} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\cdot (x+3)}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2\cdot (x+3)}}{2{e}^{(x+3)}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2\cdot (x+3)}}{2{e}^{(x+3)}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{(x+3)}}{C-{e}^{2\cdot (x+3)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above.
